The columns become shorter towards the right, forming a longer right-hand tail. The distribution is positively skewed.

examples.question_text:
A student's eight test scores were $9,6,9,6,9,5,9,4$.

Find the mean, median and mode. Which measure would the student prefer to report to make their performance appear best?
examples.solution_text:
Order the scores: $4,5,6,6,9,9,9,9$.

$\begin{aligned}\text{Mean}&=\frac{4+5+6+6+9+9+9+9}{8}\\&=\frac{57}{8}\\&=7.125\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\text{Median}&=\frac{6+9}{2}\\&=7.5\end{aligned}$

The mode is $9$, occurring four times. The student would prefer to report the mode because it is the highest of the three measures.

examples.question_text: For the scores $4,5,5,5,7,7,7,7,7$, find the mode, median and mean. Explain why the mode and median are less useful measures of centre here.
examples.solution_text:
The mode is $7$, occurring five times. There are nine ordered scores, so the median is the fifth score, also $7$.

$\begin{aligned}\text{Mean}&=\frac{4+5+5+5+7+7+7+7+7}{9}\\&=\frac{54}{9}\\&=6\end{aligned}$

The mode and median both equal the largest score, so neither represents a value between the lower and upper scores. The mean, $6$, lies between the two groups.

examples.question_text:
Consider Dataset A: $14,14,15,16,17$ and Dataset B: $14,14,15,16,117$.

Calculate each mean and explain why the mean represents Dataset A better. Would the median or mode better represent the centre of Dataset B?
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}\text{Mean of A}&=\frac{76}{5}\\&=15.2\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\text{Mean of B}&=\frac{176}{5}\\&=35.2\end{aligned}$

Dataset A's mean lies near its values. In Dataset B, the outlier $117$ pulls the mean far above the other four values.

Dataset B's median is $15$ and its mode is $14$. The median better represents the middle of the ordinary values; the mode is their lowest value.

examples.question_text:
Ten trains had delays of $0,0,0,0,0,1,2,3,6,38$ minutes.

Find the mean, median and mode. Explain which measure passengers might use to emphasise substantial delays and which measure the operator might use to present the service favourably.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}\text{Mean}&=\frac{50}{10}\\&=5\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\text{Median}&=\frac{0+1}{2}\\&=0.5\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}$

The mode is $0$ minutes.

Passengers might use the mean because it includes the severe delay of $38$ minutes. The operator might use the mode to emphasise that arriving on time is the most frequent result. The mode leaves out the size of the longer delays.

examples.question_text: A shoe store sold sizes $5,6,6,7,7,7,8,8,9,10$. Which measure of centre would help the owner decide which size to stock more of? Explain.
examples.solution_text: The mode is size $7$, occurring three times. It identifies the most frequently sold size, so it helps the owner decide which size to stock more of.

examples.question_text:
Seven employees earn $\$36{,}000$ each and one employee earns $\$436{,}000$. An advertisement reports a mean salary of $\$86{,}000$.

Check the mean and explain why it gives a misleading impression of a typical salary.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}\text{Mean salary}&=\frac{7\times36{,}000+436{,}000}{8}\\&=\frac{688{,}000}{8}\\&=86{,}000\end{aligned}$

The mean is correctly reported as $\$86{,}000$. However, seven of the eight employees earn $\$36{,}000$. The single high salary pulls the mean upwards. The median, $\$36{,}000$, better represents a typical salary.

examples.question_text:
A student's score categories were:

| Score category | Number of tests |
| --- | --- |
| 20s | 1 |
| 30s | 1 |
| 40s | 1 |
| 50s | 1 |
| 60s | 1 |
| 70s | 3 |
| 80s | 0 |
| 90s | 0 |

The student reports only that the modal category is the 70s. Explain why this can give a misleading impression.
examples.solution_text: The 70s is the modal category because it has the greatest frequency, three tests. However, five of the eight scores are below the 70s. Reporting only the modal category makes the overall performance appear stronger than it is.

examples.question_text:
The plots show scores for two groups. Is Group A generally higher scoring than Group B? Explain using clustering and skewness.

| Group A leaves | Stem | Group B leaves |
| ---: | :---: | :--- |
|  | 1 | 2 4 6 8 |
| 8 | 2 | 2 5 8 |
| 8 5 | 3 | 2 7 |
| 8 6 3 | 4 | 2 |
| 8 6 4 2 | 5 | 4 |
| 4 | 6 |  |

Key: a leaf $8$ beside stem $2$ represents $28$.
examples.solution_text: Yes. Group A clusters in the 40s and 50s, with a tail towards lower scores, so it is negatively skewed. Group B clusters in the teens and 20s, with a tail towards higher scores, so it is positively skewed. Group A's main cluster is higher.

examples.question_text:
Twenty students took a topic test before and after teaching.

| Score | Pre-test frequency | Post-test frequency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 3 | 0 |
| 1 | 7 | 1 |
| 2 | 6 | 3 |
| 3 | 3 | 6 |
| 4 | 1 | 7 |
| 5 | 0 | 3 |

Describe each distribution and explain how the scores changed.
examples.solution_text:
The pre-test distribution is positively skewed: scores cluster towards the lower end, with a tail towards higher scores.

The post-test distribution is negatively skewed: scores cluster towards the higher end, with a tail towards lower scores.

Scores generally improved after teaching.

examples.derivation: A has a longer right tail; B has a longer left tail. C has matching heights at equally spaced positions on either side of x=2.6. The classifications are positive skew, negative skew and symmetry respectively.
Successive column heights are 9, 6, 4, 2, 1 and 0.5. Frequencies taper across the right side of the highest column, supporting positive skew.

The two Bezier segments meet at the unique maximum (1.5,2.8), with horizontal tangents there. The solution places M at x=1.5 and its guide reaches that peak. The question contains no answer annotation.
Ordered scores are 4,5,6,6,9,9,9,9, totalling 57. Mean=57/8=7.125; median=(6+9)/2=7.5; mode=9 with frequency four. The mode is the highest measure.

The nine scores total 4+3×5+5×7=54, giving mean 6. The fifth ordered score is 7, also the most frequent and largest value. The explanation follows the booklet's comparison of extreme median/mode values with a mean between the groups.

Dataset A totals 76 and B totals 176, giving means 15.2 and 35.2. B's median is its third value, 15; its mode is 14. The outlier 117 raises the mean away from the four ordinary values, and the median represents their middle better than their lowest value.

Delays total 1+2+3+6+38=50, so mean=5 minutes. The fifth and sixth ordered values are 0 and 1, giving median 0.5 minutes. Zero occurs five times and is the mode. The mean includes the severe delay; the mode emphasises the most frequent result without claiming a majority.
Size 7 occurs three times, sizes 6 and 8 twice each, and the others once. The unique mode is 7, identifying the size with greatest demand in this sample.

Seven salaries total 252000; adding 436000 gives 688000. Dividing by eight gives 86000. Both middle salaries are 36000, so the median is 36000. The correctly calculated mean is elevated by the single high salary.

Frequencies total eight tests. The 70s category has the greatest frequency, three, while the five lower categories contain one test each. Thus five of eight scores fall below the reported modal category.

Group A reads 28,35,38,43,46,48,52,54,56,58,64, with seven of eleven scores in the 40s–50s and a longer lower tail. Group B reads 12,14,16,18,22,25,28,32,37,42,54, with seven of eleven in the teens–20s and a longer upper tail. A's cluster is higher, supporting the stated comparison and skew descriptions.

Each frequency column totals twenty. Pre-test frequencies peak at score 1 and taper towards higher scores; post-test frequencies are their reflection, peaking at score 4 and tapering towards lower scores. The cluster shifts upwards, supporting general improvement.
